qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Define a trade union.
items.canonical_answer: An organisation representing workers in matters such as pay and working conditions.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): an organisation representing workers’ employment interests.
objective_titles: Define a trade union

items.prompt: Identify whose interests a trade union represents and one employment matter it can raise.
items.canonical_answer: Workers’ interests; pay or working conditions.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): represents workers. Distinction/example (1): pay or working conditions.
objective_titles: Define a trade union

items.prompt: Identify two trade-union aims other than an increase in money wages.
items.canonical_answer: Improved workplace safety and greater job security.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): improved safety. Distinct example (1): greater job security.
objective_titles: Identify the aims of trade unions

items.prompt: Explain how union membership can help workers raise a shared concern about unpredictable shifts.
items.canonical_answer: Members communicate the concern, representatives combine the evidence and present a collective request, and an employer receives a clearer account of the problem. Negotiation may then produce a workable shift arrangement if agreement is feasible.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): workers raise shared concern through membership. Because/mechanism (1): representatives combine evidence. Intermediate consequence (1): clearer collective request reaches employer. Final consequence (1): discussion can improve arrangements if agreement is feasible. Total 4.
objective_titles: Describe the advantages of joining a trade union

items.prompt: Explain one advantage of representation for a worker who finds it difficult to raise a shared shift problem alone.
items.canonical_answer: A representative can bring together the worker’s concern with other members’ experiences and present it collectively, reducing reliance on the individual acting alone.
marking_guidance: Context (1): worker has difficulty raising shared concern alone. Reason/consequence (1): collective representation provides a channel to the employer.
objective_titles: Describe the advantages of joining a trade union

items.prompt: Identify the union categories associated with office occupations and with one shared skilled trade.
items.canonical_answer: White-collar union; craft union.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): office occupations indicate white-collar. Distinction (1): shared skilled trade indicates craft.
objective_titles: Describe the types of trade unions in Namibia (e.g. white collar, blue collar, craft unions)

items.prompt: Define a white-collar union.
items.canonical_answer: A union representing workers mainly in office, administrative or professional occupations.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A union representing workers mainly in office, administrative or professional occupations.
objective_titles: Describe white-collar union

items.prompt: Identify two occupational examples relevant to a white-collar union.
items.canonical_answer: Office administration and professional services.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): Office administration. Distinction/example (1): professional services.
objective_titles: Describe white-collar union

items.prompt: Define a blue-collar union.
items.canonical_answer: A union representing workers mainly in manual or industrial occupations.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A union representing workers mainly in manual or industrial occupations.
objective_titles: Describe blue-collar union

items.prompt: Identify two occupational examples relevant to a blue-collar union.
items.canonical_answer: Manual production and industrial materials handling.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): Manual production. Distinction/example (1): industrial materials handling.
objective_titles: Describe blue-collar union

items.prompt: Define a craft union.
items.canonical_answer: A union representing workers sharing a particular skilled trade.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): A union representing workers sharing a particular skilled trade.
objective_titles: Describe craft union

items.prompt: Identify two features distinguishing craft-union membership from a broad workplace grouping.
items.canonical_answer: A shared skilled trade and membership potentially drawn from several employers.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): A shared skilled trade. Distinction/example (1): membership potentially drawn from several employers.
objective_titles: Describe craft union

items.prompt: Explain how a shortage of skilled maintenance workers can strengthen their union’s bargaining position, given strong demand for employers’ output.
items.canonical_answer: Employers need the skill to meet orders, while suitable replacements are scarce. Disruption or replacement can therefore be costly, giving employers an incentive to negotiate a workable settlement. The shortage strengthens a bargaining position rather than guaranteeing a result.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): shortage of needed skill. Because/mechanism (1): replacement difficult. Intermediate consequence (1): disruption costly while orders are strong. Final consequence (1): stronger incentive to negotiate, without a guaranteed outcome. Total 4.
objective_titles: Discuss the factors affecting trade union activities in Namibia

items.prompt: Explain how weak product demand and many suitable job applicants can affect a union’s attempt to obtain a costly wage increase.
items.canonical_answer: Employers may have less ability to fund the increase and less difficulty finding alternatives, weakening the union’s bargaining position in this case.
marking_guidance: Context (1): weak demand and available applicants. Reason/conclusion (1): less scope/pressure to accept the costly demand weakens bargaining.
objective_titles: Discuss the factors affecting trade union activities in Namibia

items.prompt: Evaluate a union’s proposed wage increase where workers have scarce skills, employers have strong orders, but the rise would increase costs unless productivity also improves.
items.canonical_answer: Scarce skills and strong orders can support a settlement that improves worker income and reduces disruptive disagreement. However, higher costs can put pressure on profits, prices or labour use if productivity and revenue do not support them. Prefer a negotiated increase matched to a sustainable cost and productivity position; job losses or full acceptance cannot be assumed from the wage proposal alone.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): improved worker income (1), workable settlement can reduce disruption under strong demand (1). Argument against (2): higher labour costs (1), pressure on profits/prices/labour use (1). Condition (1): sustainable productivity/revenue relative to costs. Judgement (2): support a negotiated affordable increase (1), reject certainty about employment effects without those conditions (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Explain and evaluate the role of trade unions

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a trade union and collective bargaining.
items.canonical_answer: The union is an organisation representing workers. Collective bargaining is the negotiation process between employers or representatives and worker representatives over employment conditions.
marking_guidance: Confusion/difference (1): organisation versus process. Test to distinguish (1): identify the participant separately from the negotiation it takes part in.
objective_titles: Explain and evaluate the role of trade unions

items.prompt: Explain how an employer association can help member firms obtain suitable training where several firms report the same maintenance-skill need.
items.canonical_answer: The association collects member information, identifies the common need, combines firms’ requirements and presents them to a provider. Coordinated demand can make a relevant programme more practical if the provider has capacity and terms can be agreed.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): members report shared need. Because/mechanism (1): association gathers/coordinates information. Representation (1): common demand presented to provider. Consequence (1): suitable programme more practical under feasible capacity/terms. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain the role of employer association

items.prompt: Explain why an association presenting several workshop owners’ shared cost information in a negotiation is acting as an employer association.
items.canonical_answer: It coordinates and represents employers’ interests, rather than the interests of employees as union members.
marking_guidance: Context (1): workshop owners’ shared information represented. Reason/conclusion (1): interests are those of employers.
objective_titles: Explain the role of employer association

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between an employer association and a trade union in a wage negotiation.
items.canonical_answer: The association represents employer members; the union represents workers. Both can participate in negotiation without becoming the same organisation.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): different represented interests. Test to distinguish (1): establish whether the members are employers or workers.
objective_titles: Explain the role of employer association

items.prompt: Define trade union (2). Identify two union aims (2). Explain one role of an employer association (2). Identify the union category for office workers and for workers sharing a particular skilled trade (2).
items.canonical_answer: A trade union represents workers’ employment interests. Aims include better pay and safer conditions. An employer association coordinates member employers’ information or views so their common interests can be represented. Office workers indicate a white-collar union; a common skilled trade indicates a craft union.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): organisation (1), representing workers on employment matters (1). Separate points for aims (2): improved pay (1), safer conditions (1). Explanation (2): coordinates employers’ views (1), represents common interests (1). Identifications (2): white-collar (1), craft (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Define a trade union
Identify the aims of trade unions
Explain the role of employer association
Describe the types of trade unions in Namibia (e.g. white collar, blue collar, craft unions)

items.prompt: Invented Namibian teaching case: an association brings together workshop employers in one industry and represents their common interests. It gathers staffing and cost information. Skilled maintenance workers are difficult to replace, orders are strong, and a union seeks more predictable shifts and higher pay. Describe three features of the employer association (6). Explain how gathering and coordinating member information can improve its representation in the negotiation (7). Discuss the union’s proposed settlement, considering worker benefits, employers’ costs and the stated labour-market conditions (7).
items.canonical_answer: The association consists of employers, connects firms in the same industry and represents common interests. Collecting information establishes the members’ staffing and cost positions; comparison identifies shared concerns and differences; an agreed position can then be presented with evidence rather than inconsistent separate claims. This can improve discussion but cannot ensure agreement. Workers can benefit from pay and predictable shifts, and a settlement can reduce disruption. Strong orders and scarce skills support their position, while costs still need to be sustainable. Prefer a workable settlement linked to productivity and affordability rather than assume every wage rise reduces jobs or every demand must be accepted.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): employer members (1), not worker union membership (1); common industry (1), workshop employers stated (1); representation of interests (1), shared staffing/cost concerns (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): gather member data (1), establish actual positions (1), compare concerns (1), recognise differences (1), coordinate agreed proposal (1), present supporting evidence (1), improve discussion without ensuring agreement (1). Both sides/judgement (7): pay benefits workers (1), predictable shifts improve conditions (1), agreement can reduce disruption (1); costs may pressure firms (1); scarce skills/strong orders support bargaining (1); favour workable settlement (1) conditional on sustainable costs/productivity (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.
objective_titles: Explain the role of employer association
Discuss the factors affecting trade union activities in Namibia
Explain and evaluate the role of trade unions

items.prompt: Evaluate union bargaining in two seven-mark plans. Invented Case 1: skilled workers are scarce, employers have strong orders, and members support a request for higher pay and clearer shifts. Case 2: orders have fallen, many suitable applicants are available and the same request would substantially raise costs. Consider worker protection, bargaining conditions and possible employment effects without assuming a guaranteed result.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: representation can improve pay and shift arrangements, while a settlement protects production from disruption. Higher costs remain a disadvantage. Strong demand and scarce skills support conditional agreement if costs are sustainable. Case 2: representation remains useful for worker concerns, but weak demand and available applicants weaken leverage; an expensive settlement may pressure labour use or finances. Seek an affordable compromise, training or phased adjustment rather than assume either complete success or certain job losses.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for better worker income (1), clearer shifts/reduced disruption (1); argument against higher costs (1), possible pressure if gains unsupported (1); condition affordability under strong orders (1); judgement favours negotiation (1) because scarce skills and demand support a workable settlement (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for collective voice (1), protection of worker concerns (1); argument against weak revenue (1), available labour weakens leverage (1); condition sustainable costs and realistic alternatives (1); judgement favours compromise/phasing (1) rather than guaranteeing jobs or full acceptance (1). Total 14.
objective_titles: Discuss the factors affecting trade union activities in Namibia
Explain and evaluate the role of trade unions
